objection: There is no independent evidence of any security control today, and the knowledge base does not plan for much. Of 595 evidence requirements, 565 are first-party, 7 second-party and 23 independent-third-party. Of the 284 answer units in the security, financial-processing, legal and operational categories sampled for this review, 264 link to no independent evidence requirement at all, including every PAY, RCN, GRT, DAF, FEE, AML, TEN and IAM answer except TEN-005's planned (but unlisted) test. A bank CISO assessing a vendor that prepares payment instructions and keeps fund ledgers will tier it critical and will stop at the first two questions: where is the SOC 2 Type II, and where is the independent penetration test letter. Continuous first-party evidence, however well signed, does not answer either.
response: Add a segment-gating rule to the knowledge base: no bank or bank-affiliated sponsor engagement (including pilots with real donor data) until (a) an independent penetration test letter covering tenant isolation, authorization and payment-instruction paths and (b) at least a SOC 2 Type I exist. Add an independent evidence requirement (pen test section, SOC test of controls or agreed-upon procedures) to each answer unit that controls money movement, tenant isolation or privileged access, so that the planned answer names what will independently prove it.

objection: ANS-HR-006 is the only answer at implemented-not-independently-verified and its customer statement says work 'is attributed to the human, AI agent ... or automation that performed it'. ANS-ISP-007 and ANS-IAM-007 say the same records are self-declared and 'not authenticated identity', and the provenance blocks in this repository's own AGENTS.md record 'model: unknown'. A CISO reads HR-006 as an attribution control and ISP-007 as an admission that the control cannot be trusted. The two answers contradict each other on the one capability Echelon can currently show.
response: Change ANS-HR-006 customer statement to say the attribution is self-declared by the executing tool, not authenticated, and can be wrong or incomplete; consider partially-implemented as the status. Make the AQR contradiction check (AQR-CON-001) treat HR-006 and ISP-007 as a seeded contradiction fixture.

objection: AI agents write most of the code of a system that will prepare grant payments. The answers rely on gates and human review of 'control-relevant modules', but no answer quantifies what share of production code is agent-authored, who the human reviewers are, or whether any independent party will review the code. Bank CISOs increasingly ask exactly this, and 'some regulated buyers are uneasy regardless of controls' (SDL-006 challenge) understates it: for a critical vendor the CISO will require an independent secure code review of the money and authority paths before go-live.
response: Add an answer unit and an independent evidence requirement for a third-party white-box secure code review of control-relevant modules (gate, ledger, reservations, holds, authority, dispatch, tenant resolver) before first production data, repeated on major change. Add a disclosed metric for share of agent-authored lines per release and the identity of human approvers.

objection: Two-person controls appear throughout the target state: change review by someone other than the author, two approvers on control-relevant modules, second-person approval for privileged elevation, two-person break-glass, two-person restores, reviewer not equal to requester in AQR-REV-001, privileged access held by at least two named people. The knowledge base never states current headcount and repeatedly describes Echelon as founder-led. A CISO will ask who the second person is. If the answer is an AI agent or a not-yet-contracted advisor, every one of these controls is a design without an operator, and the target answers read as describing an organization that does not exist.
response: Add a single answer unit (and question) stating headcount, named roles and which two-person controls are operable today, with a dependency rule: any answer whose control requires two humans is tagged with the minimum staffing it needs, and AQR must not render it as planned-without-condition. Name the contracted second operator for break-glass and restores before production.

objection: The L1 to L10 assurance scale and the counts '202 rows beyond scanning, 62 complementary, 89 comparable' are Echelon's own ratings of an architecture that has no code. No bank CISO framework recognizes the scale, and no empirical test supports the 'beyond' ratings. SEC-DB-001 depends on a Strata query interface that does not exist. The report itself preserves the 'impression of precision' objection, but nothing prevents sales or AQR from quoting the counts. In a CISO review, an unsupported claim of eliminating weakness classes damages credibility more than an honest 'not yet tested'.
response: Mark the matrix and counts as internal design analysis not for customer distribution (disclosure class internal) until validated by an independent code review and pen test. When used externally, express claims only in the report's own claim structure (scope, mechanism, evidence, bypasses) and map them to recognized references (OWASP ASVS requirement IDs, NIST SSDF practices) rather than the L-scale.

objection: The scanner report concludes internally developed scanners are acceptable wherever no named qualified body is required, and the cost report lists home-built F# analyzers (H11) as a strategy. Acceptability is decided by the customer, not by the absence of an accreditation scheme. Several bank supplier standards ask for named SAST and SCA in the SDLC. With no mature F# SAST, a CISO will see a codebase that no recognized tool analyzes, plus an in-house analyzer with no track record, and will ask for compensating manual review.
response: Reword finding 5 to 'may be accepted by some customers as supplementary evidence; customer acceptance must be confirmed'. Pair the Tutela F# analyzers with an independent manual review (see OBJ-BANKCISO-003) and publish the holdout benchmark only after a third party has reviewed the method.

objection: ANS-TEN-005 has status requires-external-validation and says an independent penetration test focused on tenant isolation is performed before production, yet both linked evidence requirements are first-party. Tenant isolation is the first control a bank CISO tests in a multi-tenant sponsor platform. The evidence model cannot prove the planned control.
response: Add an independent-third-party evidence requirement for TEN-005 (cross-tenant test section of the pen test report, plus results of the customer-run two-tenant test). Apply the same rule globally: requires-external-validation answers must link at least one non-first-party evidence requirement, enforced by the build tool.

objection: The security-by-construction report finds .NET 8 and .NET 9 reached end of support on 2026-11-10 and that Strata and Ordo still target net8.0. Those are the very components cited as the basis for SEC-DB-001 and explicit-state verification. A CISO scanning a vendor's stack treats unsupported runtimes as an automatic finding, and memory-safety claims rest on a patched runtime. SEC-RUNTIME-001 is only proposed.
response: Record the out-of-support runtime as a current-state fact in the answers that cite Strata or Ordo, and make the upgrade to a supported runtime a precondition for any customer-facing claim that relies on those components.

objection: Several pen test levers will be read as steering or as reducing independence: P3 threat model handover, P5 known-issues register, P8 testing shared components once and having product tests reference that report, and P10 multi-year use of the same firm with rotation only 'every three tests' benchmarked against DORA TLPT. A bank CISO will not accept a component-level report as evidence for the Unbound product, and will ask whether known issues were excluded from testing.
response: Remove P8 as a customer-facing evidence claim (internal cost lever only). Require the attestation letter to state what material was supplied, that known issues were tested and retained in the report, and the dates of the last firm and lead-tester rotation. Cap continuous use of one firm at two annual tests before lead-tester rotation.

objection: IR-002 (roles, on-call, retained IR firm) and MON-004 (SIEM, after-hours coverage) are both unknown. The incident notification commitments (24 hours from reasonable suspicion, updates every 24 hours) and the 4-hour bank service provider trigger presuppose 24x7 detection and a staffed response. Without a contracted MDR or SOC and an IR retainer, a CISO will regard those notification commitments as unfundable promises.
response: Make a contracted 24x7 managed detection and response service and an IR retainer explicit preconditions in the target answers, with the provider listed as a subprocessor if it sees customer data, and an evidence requirement for the contracts and a test page.

objection: The most realistic compromise path for a founder-led, agent-built company is the founder's workstation and the AI engineering agents running on it with source and pipeline credentials. Endpoint controls (PHY-004) and remote work security (PHY-003) are unknown. SUB-005 covers AI providers receiving customer data, but no answer addresses AI engineering providers receiving source code, threat models, security design and pipeline tokens, which a CISO treats as a critical fourth-party exposure.
response: Add an answer unit on AI engineering provider access: which providers receive source, threat models and secrets, under what retention and training terms, with what tool permissions, and how pipeline credentials are kept out of agent sessions. Prioritize PHY-004 (managed device, EDR, disk encryption, hardware keys) as a pre-production control with evidence.

objection: Notification commitments are inconsistent. IR-004 starts the 24-hour clock at reasonable suspicion 'not confirmation'. LEG-003 commits to notify 'within 24 hours of determining that a security incident has affected or is reasonably likely to affect' data or services, a later trigger. AVL-003 notifies outages within 30 minutes of detection and DR-007 within one hour of disaster declaration. A CISO comparing the security addendum with the questionnaire will find two different triggers for the same obligation.
response: Adopt one trigger definition in a single notification matrix answer referenced by IR-004, LEG-003, AVL-003, DR-007, IR-005 and REG-007, and add the pair LEG-003/IR-004 to AQR contradiction fixtures.

objection: ANS-PAY-007 states that 'specific file encryption and account-number protection requirements are not yet written'. For a Nacha TPSP preparing payment files, a bank CISO expects file-level encryption and signing, authenticated transfer with key pinning, integrity verification end to end and segregation of payment file generation from general application roles. ENC-008 covers field encryption at rest, not payment-file integrity in transit to the ODFI.
response: Write requirements and an answer for payment file integrity and confidentiality: signed and encrypted files, transport authentication, hash comparison against the released batch, and alerting on any file not produced by the release gate.

objection: Root cloud credentials, domain registrar, code hosting ownership and signing keys appear to sit with one person. GOV-004 places break-glass credentials in sealed custody 'by a named second party' who is not named. A CISO views loss or compromise of that single person's credentials as a total-loss scenario, both for availability and for integrity of signed evidence.
response: Name the custodian and custody mechanism before production, add an independent verification (for example an escrow agent or outside counsel attestation) of the sealed custody, and include root and signing keys in the key-person register evidence.

objection: Phase 1 of the trust center publishes an 'honest-status overview' while nearly all controls are planned. TC-RED-001 blocks finding-level detail but not statements of control absence. A public page listing that logging, SIEM, IR roles, background checks and policies do not exist is reconnaissance for an attacker and will be screenshotted by competitors.
response: Keep public content to the security program approach, VDP and AI disclosure; move control-status detail to the authenticated-prospect or NDA tier. Add a redaction rule for 'absence of control' statements at the public tier.

objection: No question asks whether the vendor participates in financial-sector threat intelligence sharing (for example FS-ISAC membership or an equivalent feed), which bank CISOs commonly ask of critical vendors.
response: Add a canonical question in ISP or MON on threat intelligence sharing and how intelligence changes detections, with an answer stating current status (none) and plan.

objection: A bank CISO will require that AI features be disabled for the bank-affiliated tenant until its own AI risk review is complete.
response: Already handled: ANS-AIG-009 states each tenant can disable AI features without losing deterministic functionality, BCP-007 keeps AI out of the authoritative path, and LEG-009 makes AI use and provider change contractual. No change needed beyond keeping the disable switch evidenced.

objection: Some bank supplier standards (Morgan Stanley's documented requirement, Truist's 'unique keys unless approved') require customer-dedicated keys and FIPS-validated modules; a CISO would reject a shared-key multi-tenant design.
response: Already handled: ENC-006 and TEN-007 plan per-tenant key-encryption keys with optional customer-managed keys, and ENC-005 is precise about which operations use validated modules and makes no current FIPS claim.

objection: There is no vulnerability disclosure program today (VUL-005 unknown), yet the trust center Phase 1 lists a VDP as available now. The VDP and security.txt are cheap and expected even of pre-production vendors.
response: Publish a VDP with safe harbor and security.txt before any external marketing of Unbound, and update VUL-005 status when done.

objection: Operator access is denied by default and requires sponsor delegation, which a CISO will like, but support for a pre-revenue vendor in practice means the founder and AI support agents. SUP-005 (AI support agents) is a path to customer data that the delegation model must cover. A CISO will ask whether AI support agents can act under an OperatorAccessDelegation and what they can read.
response: State in IAM-005 and SUP-005 that AI support agents never hold operator delegations to customer data, or, if they do, that the delegation, scope and logs are visible to the sponsor exactly as for human staff.

objection: Measured against the due diligence factors in the 2023 Interagency Guidance (strategies and goals, legal and regulatory compliance, financial condition, business experience, qualifications of principals, risk management, information security, management of information systems, operational resilience, incident reporting, physical security, human resources, reliance on subcontractors, insurance, contractual arrangements with other parties), Echelon has no evidence on essentially every factor: no operating history, no financial statements, no insurance, no adopted policies, no named security officer, no background checks, no selected subcontractors. Preparing payment instructions and keeping fund ledgers for a bank-trusteed or bank-affiliated sponsor will be classified a critical activity. A vendor risk manager cannot complete a defensible file and would recommend against engagement.
response: Add to the financial-services profile an explicit verdict that Echelon is not currently eligible for bank critical-activity onboarding and a dated minimum evidence package that would make it eligible (pen test letter, SOC 2 Type I, CPA-reviewed financial statements, bound cyber/E&O/crime coverage, adopted policy set, named qualified individual, completed background checks, selected and assessed cloud provider).

objection: The question bank has no question asking how long the service has operated in production, how many customers of comparable type and size use it, and whether the vendor can provide references. This is the first business-experience question in every bank vendor intake and in the interagency guidance factor list. Its absence lets AQR route the most important negative answer to 'no match'.
response: Add canonical questions on operating history, customer count by segment and references, with an answer unit stating 'no production customers; no references' and the plan for design-partner references.

objection: The financial transparency package substitutes CPA-reviewed statements and a runway attestation signed by the managing member for audited statements. Many bank TPRM programs require audited statements for critical vendors and use third-party financial risk scores. The runway attestation is first-party and the bank confirmation proves a balance on one date, not burn or commitments. The challenge analysis calls acceptance 'uncertain', which understates that for bank-affiliated sponsors this is often a hard gate.
response: State in FST-001 that some bank programs will reject anything short of audited statements; offer CPA-reviewed statements plus agreed-upon procedures on runway and committed funding by an outside CPA as the interim, and record which target customers accept that.

objection: LEG-004 sets the data protection super-cap 'no higher than the insurance limits we actually carry', while INS-005 discloses that those limits are aggregate and shared across all customers. A VRM will read that as a cap that can be exhausted by another customer's claim. INS-001 also requires an admitted carrier, while much cyber and technology E&O capacity is written on a surplus lines basis, so the requirement may be unachievable as written.
response: Decouple the super-cap from insurance limits (state a fixed multiple of fees or fixed amount) and show the insurance as funding evidence, not the cap. Replace 'admitted carrier' with 'carrier rated A- or better by AM Best, admitted or surplus lines'.

objection: AQR-ANS-002 lets an implemented-not-independently-verified answer render as an affirmative if qualified, but many bank questionnaires are fixed picklists (Yes/No/N/A) with no room for a qualifier. In those formats the qualification is lost and the response becomes an unqualified Yes, which is a misrepresentation risk the VRM will hold the vendor to.
response: Add a rule: when the answer shape cannot carry the qualifier, the item renders as the most conservative permitted value (No or Partial) with the qualifier in a comment column or the companion ledger, and routes to human review.

objection: Bank questionnaires, security addenda and the bank's own policies are usually confidential under an NDA. AQR sends questionnaire content to external model providers for matching and drafting (steps 3 and 7). AQR-SEC-002 limits evidence artifacts sent to model providers but says nothing about the customer's questionnaire text. A VRM will treat the model provider as an undisclosed recipient of the bank's confidential information and may consider it a breach of the NDA.
response: Add AQR requirements: disclose AI processing of customer documents before upload, obtain consent or use a provider route with no retention and no training under a contract that satisfies the customer NDA, and list that provider as a recipient of customer confidential information. Add a canonical question on how the vendor handles customer-supplied questionnaires and contracts with AI tools.

objection: The knowledge base is drafted by AI research agents and no answer has had human review (AIA-007 rationale). Bank questionnaires are commonly incorporated into the contract as representations, and many require an officer signature attesting accuracy. Regulatory citations recorded as 'verified' (for example the 2026 interagency TPRM replacement proposal and the October 2025 NYDFS third-party letter) were verified by an agent fetching a page, not by counsel.
response: Before any external use: require a named human signatory per released package, a counsel review of every legal-regulatory classified answer and of customer statements that cite law, and a 'verified by' field on sources distinguishing agent retrieval from legal review.

objection: With 429 proposed-target-state and 72 unknown answer units out of 517, an honest automated response will answer 'not yet' to the large majority of a bank questionnaire. Bank TPRM scoring tools convert those into high residual risk regardless of how good the plans are. The knowledge base and AQR are designed to answer accurately, which is right, but nothing in them defines the minimum set of controls that must be operating before a questionnaire is worth submitting to a bank.
response: Define a 'minimum operating control set for financial-services submission' (for example ISP-001, ISP-002, ISP-003, IAM-001, AUN-001, ENC-001, ENC-002, VUL-001, IR-001, IR-002, BCP-001, TPR-001, HR-001, INS-001 to INS-003, PEN-001) and have AQR warn when a package targets a financial-services customer before that set reaches implemented status.

objection: The cloud provider, managed database, identity provider, email, AI providers and payment connectivity are all unselected (CLD-001 unknown, BCP-009 'no subprocessors selected'). The interagency guidance expects the bank to understand the vendor's reliance on subcontractors. A VRM cannot assess fourth-party or concentration risk, data location or carve-outs until these are chosen.
response: Record a target subprocessor list with legal entities and regions as a decision before any financial-services sales activity, and link each to an assessment record under TPR-002.

objection: EVR-ISP-010 groups 'SOC 2 Type 2 report, SOC 1 Type 2 report where relied on, or independent program assessment letter' into one independent-third-party evidence requirement. A consultant's program assessment letter is far weaker than a SOC examination, but under this record it satisfies the same evidence requirement and the trust center rule for independent badges. A VRM could be misled into treating the letter as equivalent.
response: Split EVR-ISP-010 into separate evidence requirements by assurance type (SOC 2, SOC 1, assessment letter with stated standard and scope), and allow trust center badges only for attestation reports.

objection: EVR-TPR-010 'TPRM policy and independent review report' contains independent review findings but is labeled first-party. Mixed records with a single first-party label make it impossible to tell which part is independent.
response: Split into a first-party policy record and an independent review record with its own independence label and reviewer identity.

objection: EVR-AUD-008 'Independent control sampling results' is labeled independent-third-party without stating the engagement standard, the reviewer's qualifications or what the reviewer is permitted to conclude. A semi-annual reviewer report without a professional standard is not an attestation, but under the evidence architecture and trust center rules it would display as independent assurance next to a SOC report.
response: Specify the engagement type (for example an agreed-upon procedures engagement by a CPA, or a named consultant review with stated limits), require the report to state that it is not an examination or opinion, and exclude it from 'assurance badge' display.

objection: The exit strategy that the interagency guidance expects for critical activities rests on escrow and a 'verifiable exit package'. The escrow answers are unknown, and IPR-002 says most Echelon components are licensed PolyForm Noncommercial with no commercial license yet available. A bank cannot rely on an escrow release of components it may not lawfully run in production. The exit plan is not executable today.
response: Make the commercial license grant (including on escrow release and a perpetual right to operate) a precondition for any production contract and add an evidence requirement for the signed license and an escrow agent's build verification.

objection: The ODFI's vendor management will ask the TPSP for its annual Nacha Rules compliance audit and risk assessment. The source record leaves open whether these apply to a TPSP that does not transmit files to the ODFI. Unbound's role description (prepares payment instructions and files released by the sponsor) is close enough to file preparation that the ODFI will likely expect it.
response: Resolve with counsel and the sponsor's ODFI whether the Rules compliance audit applies; until resolved, plan for an annual audit performed by an Accredited Payments Risk Professional or equivalent qualified auditor and add it to the external assurance matrix.

objection: TPR-007 aligns Echelon's program to the stages of the 2023 Interagency Guidance. The source record notes a 2026 replacement proposal with comments due 2026-12-16. The answer should not hard-code a lifecycle that may change within months.
response: Reference the guidance by lifecycle concept, note the pending proposal in TPR-007's rationale, and add a regulatory-change watch item to re-review on finalization.

objection: The amended Regulation S-P compliance dates have passed for both larger and smaller covered institutions as of this review, so any broker-dealer- or adviser-affiliated customer must already have service provider notification terms in place. IR-006 is unknown and only 'intends to meet' the 72-hour expectation. A VRM at a covered institution treats this as a must-have contract term, not an intention.
response: Convert IR-006 to a firm contractual commitment in the standard security addendum (ready before first covered-institution conversation) and set its status to proposed-target-state with the template as evidence.

objection: Background screening of personnel, including founders, is unknown. Several institutions in the profile (Fidelity documented) require background investigations including credit checks for supplier personnel with access. A VRM checks this before granting any vendor personnel access, including during implementation.
response: Complete FCRA-compliant screening of all current personnel, including founders and any contractor with repository or infrastructure access, before any customer pilot and record the evidence date.

objection: Bank audit rights cannot be flowed down to hyperscale cloud providers, so the vendor cannot honor the bank's audit and regulator access clauses.
response: Already handled: AUD-006 provides audit rights to the customer, its auditors and regulators, flows them to critical subcontractors where obtainable and, where not (large cloud providers), provides their independent reports, which is the accepted market practice.

objection: All 167 challenge analyses state customer_acceptance_likelihood (84 likely, 73 uncertain, 10 unlikely) and 134 rate the alternative 'stronger', yet none cites a source record or a customer conversation. These are first-party opinions about institutional acceptance presented in the same structure as sourced findings. A VRM reading 'Likely; regulators and auditors recognize...' will ask for the basis.
response: Add a required basis field to the challenge schema (source IDs or 'author judgment, unvalidated'), set every current value to 'author judgment, unvalidated', and require at least two target-customer conversations or a sourced document before any value is raised to 'likely'.

objection: Bank data processing terms (Morgan Stanley's published terms are an example) require prior written consent per subprocessor rather than notice with a right to object. SUB-002 offers 30 days' notice and an objection right, which a bank VRM will redline.
response: Add a contract option for prior written consent for bank customers, supported by the per-tenant subprocessor selection already proposed in SUB-002's challenge analysis.

objection: First-party reports could be shown on the trust center in a way that a reviewer mistakes for independent assurance.
response: Already handled: TC-HON-002 requires independence labels and forbids calling an attestation a certification, badges require an evidence record with independence independent-third-party, and first-party assessments carry a 'First-party assessment' label. See OBJ-VRM-010 and OBJ-VRM-012 for the two evidence records that still need separation.

objection: The assurance timeline is internally inconsistent and, as written, not achievable. AUD-001 plans SOC 2 Type I then Type II 'after production launch'. FCT-004 and RCN-005 require a SOC 1 Type 2 covering ledger posting, NAV, reconciliation, change and access 'before the first hosted sponsor's fiscal year end'. A Type 2 report needs controls placed in operation and a period of operation (in practice rarely less than three months, and user auditors generally want coverage of most of their fiscal year), followed by fieldwork and issuance. Unless go-live precedes the first sponsor's fiscal year end by roughly six to nine months, the first sponsor's auditor will have no SOC 1 Type 2 to rely on and will need to test Unbound directly or substantively.
response: Write one assurance roadmap answer that sequences: readiness, SOC 2 Type I and SOC 1 Type 1 as of go-live, first Type 2 periods sized to the first sponsor's fiscal year, and a stated fallback (sponsor auditor direct testing at Echelon's cost or substantive procedures). Make AUD-001, AUD-002, FCT-004 and RCN-005 reference it instead of stating separate timing.

objection: The external assurance matrix lists 17 activities and has no SOC 1 row, and the cost avoidance report's 'cannot be avoided' table omits SOC 1, although AUD-002, FCT-004 and RCN-005 commit to a SOC 1 Type 2. A SOC 1 is a separate examination with control objectives, a separate system description and its own fees. The cost picture understates the largest recurring assurance cost a fund administration platform faces.
response: Add EXT rows for SOC 1 Type 1 and Type 2 (independent CPA, AT-C 320, restricted use) with cost evidence or 'unknown', and add SOC 1 to the unavoidable items table in DD-COST-002.

objection: AUD-001 places Processing Integrity in the SOC 2 scope for Unbound. Sponsors' financial statement auditors rely on SOC 1 control objectives, not on SOC 2 Processing Integrity criteria, so Processing Integrity adds scope and cost without satisfying user auditors, while SOC 2 security and availability serve TPRM reviewers. Doing both SOC 2 with PI and SOC 1 duplicates testing of the same transaction controls.
response: Make SOC 1 the primary report for transaction processing and SOC 2 (Security, Availability, Confidentiality) the TPRM report; add Processing Integrity only if a customer contract requires it. Ask the CPA firm about a combined engagement to reduce duplicated testing.

objection: Trust Services Criteria CC1.2 asks whether the board of directors (or equivalent) demonstrates independence from management and exercises oversight. Echelon has a managing member who is management, risk acceptor and policy approver, and only a planned advisory board without authority. The auditor will evaluate whether governance is designed to meet CC1.2 and whether segregation-dependent controls operate. In a one-principal organization the likely outcome is exceptions or a description that relies heavily on outside parties.
response: Before the examination period, constitute a body with actual oversight authority (for example a board of managers with an independent member, or a contracted independent advisor with documented authority to escalate), and record how CC1.2 and CC1.3 are met with evidence.

objection: A service auditor tests automated controls by evaluating IT general controls and testing the control once (baselining). An LLM agent is not deterministic, so a control performed by an AI agent cannot be baselined and must be tested like a manual control, with evidence of each performance and of human review. AIA-006 correctly keeps evidence generation deterministic, but other answers describe agents operating, monitoring and remediating. The knowledge base never classifies which key controls an AI agent performs.
response: Add a performer field to each control (deterministic software, human, AI agent with human review) and a rule that no key control in SOC scope is performed solely by an AI agent; disclose agent-performed activities in the system description.

objection: The design treats hashes, population counts, query definitions and DSSE signatures as information-produced-by-entity support. A signature proves that a record has not changed since signing; it does not prove the population was complete or the query correct. To rely on IPE the auditor must test the logic and the ITGCs over the generating systems, which here are Echelon's own Praxis, Tutela, Dokimos and Strata. Those tools then enter the examination scope. H4 (fewer auditor requests) may reverse in the first years.
response: State in DD-ARC-003 and H4 that evidence tooling becomes in-scope systems requiring ITGC testing, and plan the first examination with an explicit assumption that custom evidence increases first-year auditor hours. Agree the reliance approach with the CPA firm before building (already listed as a substitution risk; make it a gating decision).

objection: CHG-006's challenge rates auditor acceptance of 'evidence by construction from work protocol' as likely. Praxis actor attribution is self-declared. An auditor testing change authorization will rely on authenticated approvals enforced by the source control platform (branch protection, required reviewers bound to IdP identities), not on a repository-written provenance record that the author's own tooling produces.
response: Downgrade the acceptance rating to uncertain and state that Praxis provenance is supplementary; the change-control evidence of record is the source-control platform's enforced settings and approval logs, with Praxis linking work items.

objection: Verification criterion V-11 sets independent_of_implementation to true when 'the signer and actor differ from the change author'. In a founder-led company the signer may be a CI identity or an AI agent controlled by the same person who authored the change. Different identity is not independence in the auditing sense. The field will mark records independent that an auditor would regard as self-review.
response: Rename the field to signer_differs_from_author, or require that the independent signer be a human (or organization) outside the author's reporting line recorded in a role registry, and forbid deriving any independence label from AI or CI identities.

objection: FCT-007 and PAY-008 say a deterministic release gate counts as an approver only after 'the auditor and board have accepted the design' (CNV-GOV-003). A service auditor does not approve or accept a control design in advance; designing and approving controls is a management responsibility and taking it on would threaten the auditor's independence under the AICPA nonattest services provisions. A user auditor may document a planned reliance approach but does not accept a vendor's design either.
response: Replace 'auditor acceptance' with 'management-approved design, sponsor board adoption, and a documented user-auditor planned approach', and state that the service auditor evaluates design and operating effectiveness only within an examination.

objection: The external assurance matrix leaves unknown whether a CPA firm that performs readiness can later perform the examination. AUD-007 also proposes an 'external reviewer' testing controls semi-annually, and the cost report proposes internal readiness. If the same CPA firm provides readiness, policy drafting, the semi-annual testing or tooling advice and then the examination, independence must be evaluated under the AICPA Code's nonattest services rules. This is a known pitfall for small first-time service organizations.
response: Research and record the AICPA independence position (Code of Professional Conduct, nonattest services) and adopt a rule: the examining firm performs no management functions, policy authoring or control design; readiness, if purchased, goes to a different firm or is limited to permitted services.

objection: The trust center research places a SOC 1 Type II at the NDA tier. A SOC 1 report is restricted to the management of the service organization, its user entities and the user entities' auditors; prospects are not intended users. (SOC 2 permits distribution to prospective users with sufficient knowledge, so NDA gating is appropriate there.) TC-TIER-003 auto-approval of NDA artifacts for allowlisted domains could therefore distribute a SOC 1 outside its restriction.
response: Add a requirement that SOC 1 reports are available only to the existing-customer tier (and the customer's auditor via the auditor tier), never auto-approved, and that each report's own use restriction paragraph drives its tier.

objection: AUD-003 plans report periods so the gap to 'customers' common fiscal year ends' does not exceed three months. DAF sponsors have different fiscal years (June 30 is common among national sponsors and many community foundations use December 31). One annual period cannot serve both with a three-month gap. AUD-003 also supplements bridge letters with continuous first-party evidence, which adds no assurance in the user auditor's evaluation.
response: State the fiscal year ends of target sponsors and either use two reporting periods or a six-month cadence; describe continuous evidence as information, not assurance, in the bridge letter answer.

objection: Many Unbound controls rely on sponsor actions: board resolutions, dual or triple payment release, sanctions alert disposition, controller sign-off, out-of-band payment recording, and residual risk acceptance for small sponsors that cannot segregate duties. These become complementary user entity controls. If they are numerous and demanding, user auditors must test them at each sponsor and small sponsors may not operate them, which weakens the value of the SOC 1 to those sponsors.
response: Draft the CUEC list now from the requirements, rate each by sponsor effort, and validate with two prospective sponsors that they can operate them; publish it in AUD-001 and AUD-002 target answers.

objection: CLD-004 addresses carve-out of the cloud provider, but the system description will also have to address AI model providers used in the product and in operations, and Echelon's own PolyForm-licensed tooling if it produces in-scope evidence. AI providers' SOC reports typically cover infrastructure and security of the service, not model behavior, so complementary subservice organization controls for AI are thin.
response: List AI providers as subservice organizations in CLD-009, record which of their reports exist and what they cover, and state the Unbound controls that compensate for model behavior (deterministic gates, human approval).

objection: AUD-001 says controls emit evidence as a byproduct 'so the observation period is cheap to evidence'. The cost of a Type 2 is driven mainly by the auditor's procedures, sampling and reporting, not by the vendor's evidence collection. 'Cheap' is unsupported and contradicts the cost report's hypothesis framing.
response: Replace 'cheap to evidence' with 'expected to reduce internal evidence preparation effort (hypothesis H4, unmeasured)'.

objection: Several challenge analyses treat continuous automation as replacing periodic review or sampling (INF-007: daily zero-drift attestations 'replace sampling'; FEE-002: full-population recomputation 'instead of sampling', rated likely). Auditors may reduce sample sizes when an automated control is tested effective with ITGCs, but they still perform procedures and will not accept the entity's own attestations in place of testing.
response: Reword these alternatives to 'supports reduced auditor sampling where the automated control and its ITGCs are tested effective' and set acceptance to uncertain until the CPA firm confirms.

objection: The only policy is a proposed Secure Construction Standard that assigns roles to systems that do not perform them (Aegis as security rule registry, Vigila as runtime monitoring, per the current-state brief). If adopted as written, the system description and policies would describe controls that do not exist, a misstatement the auditor must report. Policies must also be in effect for the whole examination period.
response: Correct system ownership in the Standard before adoption (already recommended), adopt the policy set at least one full period before the planned Type 2 start, and add a check that every policy statement maps to an existing operating mechanism or is marked aspirational and excluded from the system description.

objection: With no or very few sponsors in the first observation period, many controls will have no occurrences: terminations, incidents, payee changes, disbursements, returns, emergency changes. Reports full of 'no instances occurred, no testing performed' give user auditors little to rely on for transaction controls, which is exactly what a SOC 1 is for.
response: Plan the first SOC 1 as a Type 1 at go-live and set the first Type 2 period to begin only when transaction volume can support testing; tell design-partner sponsors in advance that their first year's audit may need direct testing.

objection: Section 8 notes all proposed evidence producers except the Registry are PolyForm Noncommercial and that reproducing a producer's observation requires a license. Reperformance is a standard audit procedure; a commercial CPA firm may not be able to run the tool lawfully to reperform.
response: Grant the examining firm a written license for audit reperformance (REC-ORGADMIN-002) and record it as a precondition of the engagement.

objection: Marketing could describe Echelon as 'SOC 2 certified' or 'SOC 2 compliant' before a report is issued.
response: Already handled: TC-HON-002 forbids calling an attestation a certification, AUD-001 commits not to claim compliance before an auditor issues a report, and AUD-008 generates every public assurance statement from a single assurance record limited to the issued report's type, period and scope.

objection: An examiner evaluates the bank, not the vendor. If a bank (or a bank acting as trustee of a charitable gift fund) engaged Echelon today for a critical activity, the examiner would review the bank's due diligence file and find no independent assurance, no audited financials, no operating history, a single key person, no incident response capability and unadopted policies. The likely outcome is criticism of the bank's third-party risk management, possibly a matter requiring attention. Banks know this and will not engage. The knowledge base frames bank requirements as flowing to Echelon but never states this examiner-side consequence, which is what actually ends the sale.
response: Add to the financial-services profile and TPR-007 an explicit examiner-perspective statement: what a bank must be able to show an examiner about Echelon for a critical activity, and which items are missing today.

objection: The profile documents that Bank of America, N.A. is sole trustee of the Bank of America Charitable Gift Fund. When a national bank administers a charitable fund as trustee, that is a fiduciary activity examined by the OCC under 12 CFR Part 9 and the OCC's asset management guidance, and state-chartered trust companies face analogous state rules. Outsourcing administration of a fiduciary account raises the bank's duties over the vendor and its records. The knowledge base contains no reference to 12 CFR Part 9 or trust fiduciary examination and no question for bank-trustee sponsors.
response: Add a source record for 12 CFR Part 9 (and a note on state trust company analogues), a canonical question on support for the trustee bank's fiduciary oversight and recordkeeping, and an answer unit marked requires-external-validation pending counsel review.

objection: IR-005 commits to notify 'each affected bank customer's designated contacts'. The 2021 computer-security incident notification rule also provides that if the bank has not designated a contact, the service provider notifies the bank's chief executive officer and chief information officer, or two individuals with comparable responsibilities. The fallback is missing, and IR-005 is status unknown even though it is a binding regulatory requirement whenever Echelon is a bank service provider.
response: Add the default-contact fallback to IR-005 and REG-007, move IR-005 to proposed-target-state with an onboarding control that refuses activation for a bank tenant without verified designated contacts.

objection: GOV-007's target answer states that Echelon 'is not a bank, money transmitter, investment adviser or broker-dealer because the platform never holds, controls or executes movement of customer funds, which is enforced by architecture'. REG-001 and AML-006 say counsel has not confirmed this. Architecture is a fact input to the legal analysis; it does not settle state money transmission definitions, adviser status when allocation options and rebalancing workflows are presented, or whether a regulator views payment-file preparation as transmission. A target answer that states the legal conclusion invites AQR to emit it.
response: Rewrite GOV-007 target to 'Echelon's position, subject to counsel opinion, is ...' and add an independent evidence requirement (legal opinion by state and federal regime) shared by GOV-007, REG-001, INV-001 and AML-006.

objection: All answer units with status requires-external-validation except two (AUZ-007, ISP-008) link only first-party evidence requirements. The validation they need, legal opinions for AML-006, DAF-010, AIG-007 and WLB-002 and an independent test for TEN-005, has no evidence requirement, so the knowledge base cannot show when the validation happened or who gave it.
response: Add counsel-opinion and independent-test evidence requirements (independence second-party or independent-third-party as appropriate) and add a build rule that requires-external-validation answers must link one.

objection: OFAC sanctions are strict liability for U.S. persons, and Echelon is a U.S. person. AML-001 and AML-002 treat screening as a sponsor service, and REG-004 covers screening Echelon's owners, vendors and customers. Neither addresses Echelon's own exposure if it prepares or transmits a payment instruction that benefits a blocked person, for example through a stale list or a matcher defect, nor whether Echelon must itself block or report.
response: Extend REG-004 with counsel analysis of Echelon's own OFAC exposure as a service provider in the payment chain, its blocking and reporting duties if any, and a voluntary self-disclosure procedure; reference it from AML-002's fail-closed design.

objection: The financial-services profile records that large banking organizations flow down resolution-planning requirements: continuity of service during the customer's resolution, no termination or suspension triggered by the resolution, and assignment to successors. No answer unit commits to these terms; LEG-006 covers termination by the customer and on Echelon's insolvency, not service continuity through the customer's resolution.
response: Add a canonical question and extend LEG-006 or TRM-004 with resolution-resilient terms (no termination for resolution events while fees are paid, assignment to a bridge entity or acquirer, continued data access) marked applicable to systemically important banking customers.

objection: Echelon would not acknowledge that its services to banks are examinable under the Bank Service Company Act, leaving the bank unable to meet examiner expectations.
response: Already handled: REG-003 commits to contractually acknowledge 12 U.S.C. 1867(c) examination authority, to support the bank's notice of the service relationship and to cooperate with examinations, and DDQ-REG-0010 asks the question.

objection: A bank examiner applying model risk management expectations (SR 11-7 and OCC 2011-12) would find no support for validating vendor models such as sanctions match scoring.
response: Already handled: AIG-008 classifies components a bank would treat as models and plans a model documentation package with evaluation results and change notice; AML-003 adds measured recall on a versioned perturbation suite. The remaining gap (no model exists yet) is a status issue, not a design gap.

objection: Sanctions recordkeeping periods may be stated using the old five-year OFAC period.
response: Already handled: AML-005 retains screening and disposition records for at least ten years, consistent with OFAC's extended recordkeeping period, by reference to CNV-PLT-004.

objection: Several recent regulatory items on which answers depend are recorded as verified by agent retrieval and are too recent for this reviewer to confirm independently: the 2026 interagency TPRM replacement proposal (91 FR 58536) and its comment extension, the October 2025 NYDFS third-party service provider industry letter, the Nacha 2026 rules edition and fraud monitoring phases, and the FFIEC Outsourcing booklet whose status is recorded as unknown. If any detail is wrong, the regulatory-driven requirements in the financial-services profile would be misstated to customers.
response: Have counsel or a compliance professional reverify each of these against the issuing agency's own publication before any customer use, and record the reviewer and date in the source record separately from agent verification.

objection: The FFIEC Development, Acquisition, and Maintenance booklet (August 2024) and the Architecture, Infrastructure, and Operations booklet (June 2021) are recorded as sources, but the SDL, CHG and INF answers map to SSDF and SOC 2 rather than to the examination areas an examiner would actually use for a bank's oversight of a technology service provider.
response: Add DAM and AIO booklet locators to the relevant SDL, CHG, INF and BCP answers (by section, not quoted text) so a bank can map vendor evidence to its examination workpapers.

objection: No question or answer addresses unfair or deceptive acts or practices in donor-facing experiences. Echelon is a for-profit company and is subject to Section 5 of the FTC Act for its own representations, and state attorneys general police charitable solicitation and platform conduct. White-label donor portals, fee displays, tax-deductibility statements and AI-generated communications are where such claims arise.
response: Add canonical questions on donor-facing claims review (fees, deductibility, recognition, AI content), dark-pattern avoidance and complaint handling, with an answer unit tied to DON-005 and WLB-001 and counsel review of templates.

objection: An examiner who uses BSCA authority, or who examines a covered customer, expects records within short timeframes and access to knowledgeable personnel. With one principal, examiner availability, document production and interviews during an incident or year-end conflict directly with operations. RET-006 (recordkeeping obligations of regulated customers) is unknown.
response: Add an examination-readiness answer: designated regulatory liaison and backup, target production times for standard evidence packages, and a resolved RET-006 that maps sponsor-affiliate recordkeeping obligations to Unbound retention.

objection: No rule prohibits AI-authored code at a bank service provider, but an examiner reviewing a bank's oversight of a critical vendor will ask how the bank satisfied itself that change management, testing and access controls over AI-written code are effective. The knowledge base relies on first-party provenance and unbuilt gates and has no independent verification of agent controls planned beyond the SOC 2 (SOC2-017).
response: Add an independent evidence requirement specific to agent controls (for example a scoped assessment of agent permissions, gate bypass resistance and human review coverage) and reference it from SDL-006, ISP-007 and AIA-008.

objection: Echelon has not determined whether GLBA applies, so a bank cannot rely on it to meet the Interagency Guidelines' service provider safeguards requirement.
response: Already handled: PRV-003 treats donor financial data as nonpublic personal information regardless of status, accepts service provider safeguards terms that bank customers need under the Interagency Guidelines and maintains an information security program meeting FTC Safeguards Rule elements regardless of status.

objection: Concentration and continuity risk from the examiner's side: if several sponsors, including bank-affiliated ones, depend on one founder-operated vendor, the failure of that one person is a correlated event across institutions. The challenge analysis for BCP-005 relies on portability and exit packages, but a bank examiner evaluates whether the bank can actually transition within its tolerance, and no successor operator or transition provider exists.
response: Name a contracted successor operator or transition partner with documented ability to run Unbound from escrow, test it annually with customer observation, and state this in BCP-005 and GOV-004 as a precondition for bank-affiliated customers.

objection: Nacha's risk-based fraud monitoring requirements for TPSPs and Originators are network rules enforced through the ODFI, not a regulation, but bank examiners review the ODFI's oversight of its third-party participants. Unbound's fraud monitoring program is a precondition for rail activation in the design but does not exist, and the sponsor's ODFI will ask for it at onboarding.
response: Keep FRD-008 as a go-live precondition and add an ODFI-facing evidence package (program document, annual review record) to its evidence requirements.

objection: A sponsor board approving a change of its core administration platform must document a prudent selection. Unbound has no code in production, no customers, no operating history, no audited financials, no insurance and one key person. A national sponsor's board would not move donor accounts and grant processing to it, and a bank-affiliated sponsor's board would be overruled by the parent's TPRM in any case. The knowledge base contains every ingredient of this conclusion but never states it as a verdict for the DAF segment.
response: Add a segment readiness statement to the DAF profile: Unbound is presently suitable only for a design-partner arrangement with a sponsor that keeps its incumbent system of record, with stated exit criteria to production use (independent assurance, financial and insurance package, successor operator, completed parallel run).

objection: No question or answer covers conversion from the sponsor's incumbent administrator: extracting historical funds, contributions with gift dates and cost basis, grants and their states, succession plans, advisor privileges, recurring grants, documents and audit history, reconciling converted balances to the incumbent's records and the audited financial statements, and running in parallel through at least one close. For a CFO this is the largest project risk of switching, larger than any steady-state control.
response: Add canonical questions and an answer unit on data conversion and parallel run (conversion reconciliation tolerances, sign-off, rollback plan, handling of in-flight grants at cutover, donor communication), with evidence requirements for the conversion reconciliation report.

objection: The FEE category is about the sponsor's fees to donors. No question addresses what Echelon charges the sponsor: pricing model, implementation fees, price escalators, minimums, cost of dedicated isolation profiles or customer-managed keys, and cost of the sponsor-side staffing the design requires. FEE-006 admits Echelon's revenue model is not established. A CFO cannot compare Unbound with an incumbent without it.
response: Add canonical questions on Echelon's commercial terms and total cost of ownership to the sponsor, and an answer unit with status unknown until pricing is decided.

objection: DAF-009 promises deterministic gates against taxable distributions, prohibited benefits and excess benefit transactions. If a platform defect lets one through, section 4966 imposes excise tax on the sponsoring organization and on fund managers who agreed knowing it was taxable, section 4967 on donors, advisors and fund managers, and section 4958 on disqualified persons and managers. None of that liability shifts to Echelon. No question or answer addresses whether Echelon indemnifies the sponsor for excise taxes, correction costs and donor remediation caused by its own defect, and LEG-004's cap would limit any recovery.
response: Add a canonical question on allocation of excise tax and correction costs caused by platform error, and extend LEG-004 with a position (for example a specific indemnity outside the general cap for errors in deterministic compliance gates, funded by E&O), reviewed by counsel.

objection: The sponsor CFO's external audit fee and timeline depend on whether a SOC 1 Type 2 exists. FCT-004 acknowledges that until one exists the sponsor's auditor must test Unbound directly or substantively. The audit committee will ask who pays for that additional audit work and whether the auditor will even accept direct testing of a vendor's systems in the first year. The answers do not address cost allocation.
response: State in FCT-004 that, until a SOC 1 Type 2 covers the sponsor's fiscal year, Echelon will fund or credit the incremental audit procedures and provide on-site or remote access for the sponsor's auditor, and add a canonical question on audit-cost impact.

objection: The source record for IRC 170 notes Pub. L. 119-21 added a non-itemizer charitable deduction under section 170(p) that excludes contributions to establish or maintain a DAF, and a 0.5 percent floor for itemizers. No question or answer unit uses this. Donor-facing contribution flows, acknowledgments, marketing and AI-generated communications on a white-label DAF platform are exactly where a donor could be misled into thinking a DAF gift qualifies for the new deduction, which is a reputational and regulatory risk for the sponsor.
response: Add a canonical question on donor-facing deductibility statements after the 2025 changes, and update CON-007 and DON-005 targets to require counsel-approved deductibility language that excludes DAF gifts from the 170(p) deduction.

objection: DAF contribution and receipting volume concentrates in the last weeks of December. A first year-end on a new platform with no production history is the highest-risk moment for a sponsor: late gift dates, missed acknowledgments and failed grants damage donor relationships and tax outcomes. The knowledge base specifies freeze periods and performance targets, but no answer commits to load evidence at December volumes or to keeping the incumbent available through the first year-end.
response: Add to PRF and BCP a precondition that a sponsor's first year-end on Unbound follows a successful parallel run and a load test at a documented multiple of that sponsor's prior December peak, with the incumbent kept as fallback.

objection: From the sponsor CFO's seat, the build-instead-of-buy program (own compliance monitoring H10, own F# analyzers H11, generated trust center, AQR, evidence architecture, CWE matrix) is a very large engineering agenda for a vendor that has not yet built its core product. Whatever these save in license fees, they compete for the same scarce founder and agent time as the fund accounting, payments and conversion work the sponsor is buying. The savings are labeled hypotheses, but the opportunity cost to delivery is not quantified at all.
response: Add an explicit sequencing rule to DD-COST-002: no internal assurance tooling beyond what the first SOC examination and first pen test require until Unbound's core is in production, and quantify engineering hours diverted in the TCO table.

objection: The board's main protection against vendor failure is a funded wind-down, verified escrow with a usable license and a successor operator. FST-003 is planned, TRM-003 and the escrow answers are unknown, IPR-002 says no commercial license exists yet, and no wind-down reserve is evidenced. The challenge analysis rates escrow-plus-export as 'likely' acceptable to DAF sponsors; that is plausible only once those pieces exist and have been tested with the sponsor observing.
response: Lower the FST-003 acceptance rating to uncertain until the escrow agreement, commercial license, reserve amount and first observed exit rehearsal exist, and add the reserve to EVR-FST-006 with an outside accountant's confirmation.

objection: A national sponsor administers billions of dollars of fund assets. A systematic fee, unitization or NAV error across all funds, or a fraudulent grant released through a compromised workflow, can exceed any E&O or crime limit a startup can buy, and LEG-004 caps liability at fees or insurance limits. The CFO will conclude the sponsor keeps essentially all the financial risk of the platform.
response: State plainly in INS-002 and LEG-004 that achievable limits are small relative to sponsor assets, quantify the largest plausible loss scenarios, and describe the sponsor-side controls (sponsor release authority, reconciliation, own crime coverage) that keep losses within those limits.

objection: PAY-008 requires three distinct people to release a payment until a deterministic gate is accepted, and GRT-002 requires a board resolution before policy-based approval. National sponsors process very large grant volumes with lean staff; community foundations may have two or three finance staff in total. The default is operationally unworkable for both, and RCN-004's acceptance of residual risk for small sponsors contradicts PAY-008's hard rule.
response: Define release-control tiers by amount and risk (for example two-person release under a threshold with post-release independent review, three-person above), reconcile PAY-008 with RCN-004, and test the staffing assumption with two prospective sponsors.

objection: The TPSP-only model makes the sponsor the Originator under its own ODFI agreement, with mandatory positive pay and sponsor-side return handling. Many community foundations do not have ACH origination agreements and would need to obtain them, with bank fees, underwriting and their own Nacha obligations. This cost and effort sits with the sponsor and is not visible in the answers' cost fields, which describe only Echelon's cost.
response: Add sponsor-side prerequisites and their approximate cost drivers to PAY-001 (ODFI agreement, positive pay, return handling staff), and add a canonical question asking what banking arrangements the sponsor must have in place.

objection: OQ-DD-TC-002 asks whether a trust center full of 'planned' items helps or hurts with DAF sponsors and proposes two sponsor conversations. Until answered, Phase 1 publication is a bet. Sponsors' boards and their donors may read a public list of absent controls as a reason not to proceed, and competitors may cite it.
response: Do not publish Phase 1 publicly until the two sponsor conversations are held; use the authenticated-prospect tier in the meantime.

objection: The profile concludes the incumbent assurance baseline is 'modest' because one administrator publicly cites a SOC 2 Type 1, and that a SOC 2 Type II would be differentiating. That conflates assurance artifacts with institutional acceptance. Incumbents also bring years of operating history, operations staff, sponsor references, conversion experience and parent-institution relationships. A Type II alone will not displace them.
response: Revise implication 5 to list the non-assurance factors on which incumbents lead and to state that a SOC 2 Type II is necessary but not sufficient.

objection: AIG-009 commits to publish that 'Echelon builds its software largely with AI coding agents'. For a sponsor whose brand rests on donor trust, a public statement that its giving platform was largely written by AI may raise donor and board questions irrespective of controls. White-label sponsors may not want the statement on their branded properties.
response: Keep the disclosure to sponsors in contracting and on Echelon's own trust center, and let white-label sponsors decide whether donor-facing pages carry it, while keeping in-product AI content labeling.

objection: FEE-003 records that advance donor notice of fee changes is not specified in Unbound requirements. Sponsors' donor agreements and program circulars commonly promise notice before fee increases, and a platform that can change fees without enforcing notice is a donor-relations and potentially a misrepresentation risk.
response: Add the advance-notice gate to Unbound requirements via recommendations and change FEE-003 target to enforce a sponsor-configured minimum notice period.

objection: Bank-affiliated and broker-affiliated sponsors typically use an affiliate as investment manager. INV-006 says UPMIFA applicability to DAF assets has not been analyzed by counsel, and FEE-006 notes Echelon's own revenue model and related-party relationships are undisclosed. A board will ask whether Unbound's investment workflows and any revenue arrangements create conflicts it must manage.
response: Add counsel analysis of UPMIFA and prudent-investor duties as they bear on platform reporting, and commit to disclose any Echelon revenue arrangement with investment managers or custodians before contracting.

objection: A sponsor board may worry that automation erodes its exclusive legal control and variance power over DAF assets.
response: Already handled: DAF-007 makes reserved authority holdable only by persons appointed by board resolution and excludes vendor staff and AI agents, GRT-002 requires a board resolution before any policy-based approval, and AML-004 lets only authorized humans dispose of sanctions alerts.

objection: No question asks for an implementation plan: timeline, sponsor staff effort, policy configuration workload (DAF-006 requires every sponsor policy to be declared and versioned), training and go-live criteria. For a CFO this is a key input to the decision and the budget.
response: Add canonical questions on implementation plan and sponsor effort, with an answer stating that no implementation methodology yet exists.
